source.title: Adam Induces Implicit Weight Sparsity in Rectifier Neural Networks
source.authors: A. Yaguchi; Taiji Suzuki; Wataru Asano; Shuhei Nitta; Y. Sakata; A. Tanizawa

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; figure values are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on optimizer, activation, regularization, network width and depth, and measured sparsity/activation properties that bear on optimizer generalization and measured properties tracking the train–test gap. Its focus is implicit sparsity rather than the claim’s generalization outcomes, and it does not measure train–test gaps.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation accuracy and weight-vector sparsity, not training error versus test error or held-out error against chance. Its optimizer comparisons therefore do not test the V4 held-out-performance claim. The reported sparsity and activation-rate results bear on measured network properties but do not establish that they track a generalization gap.
record.test_reason: The study tests V4 through its own optimizer comparisons on MNIST and CIFAR-10. Validation accuracy measures held-out performance; training–test gaps are not required for V4. Its sparsity measurements address a different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors attribute implicit group sparsity to Adam, ReLU and L2 regularization, analyze rapid decay under restricted conditions, and propose pruning near-zero weight vectors. Their theorem does not establish unconditional convergence to zero. They also report an Adam–mSGD validation-accuracy gap on CIFAR-10 and speculate that implicit sparsity contributes to it.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies implicit weight sparsity and model reduction with validation accuracy and sparsity measures; it does not compare training error with test error or measure a generalization gap.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer, activation function, L2 regularization, batch normalization, initializer, width, depth and dataset affect the reported sparsity and validation-accuracy outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimizer, activation function and L2 regularization strongly affect weight-vector sparsity, despite similar MNIST validation accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adam or RMSprop with suitable activations and L2 regularization can produce near-zero incoming weight vectors.

fits_no_version.finding: Networks with 500, 1000 and 2000 hidden nodes retain about 288–300 nodes and achieve similar validation accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under this regularized MNIST recipe, wider networks can converge to similar retained sizes and held-out accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Depth changes validation accuracy and the distribution of retained nodes across layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Implicit pruning varies with network depth and layer position in these MNIST networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected CIFAR-10 filters show jointly declining activation rates and weight norms with Adam, while mSGD maintains nonzero values.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adam-associated weight decay and declining ReLU activity can occur together in selected filters.

fits_no_version.finding: Adam reduces 53.23% of CIFAR-10 network parameters, whereas mSGD, AMSGRAD and AdamW do not induce comparable sparsity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Implicit parameter sparsity depends on the optimizer and its treatment of weight decay.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications (2018)
record.problems: The experiments report validation accuracy and sparsity, not train–test gaps or random-label controls. Figure-only trajectories provide no numerical values in the supplied text. The CIFAR optimizer comparison reports a maximum validation accuracy over training and gives no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out; all extracted table and figure findings are included.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, chance-level held-out performance under random labels, and comparison with natural-label generalization.
Width beyond an established zero-training-error threshold, with convergence and no explicit regularization.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected comparisons, local connectivity, and convolution-derived initialization.
Equal or better training performance, language benchmarks, broader hyperparameter searches, and switching from Adam to SGD. No learning-rate tuning search is documented.
Batch-size comparisons and adaptations to large batches.
Dropout ablations, small-data regimes, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, measured generalization gaps, and rankings against norm- or margin-based measures.
Memorization-based example removal and comparison with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: The record incorrectly excludes validation accuracy as evidence of held-out performance. Optimizer comparisons test V4 even without training-error measurements. CIFAR-10 results are maxima over 400 epochs and lack uncertainty estimates; the documented learning rates are specified settings rather than a reported tuning search. Model-reduction comparisons in Section V-B do not isolate optimizer generalization because the regularizers and methods differ.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected test-error comparisons.
Held-out performance comparison between adaptive optimizers and SGD; only validation accuracy and sparsity are reported.
Large-batch versus small-batch held-out performance and adaptations to batch size.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to training–test gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-10 VGG-style network, 400 epochs, specified optimizer learning rates and common training recipe
relationships.reason: R23–R26 report mSGD at 93.13%, above AMSGRAD at 92.64%, AdamW at 91.97%, and Adam at 92.61%; the authors explicitly identify the Adam–mSGD accuracy gap.
relationships.display_finding: Reported accuracy favored mSGD over AMSGRAD, AdamW, and Adam under the specified recipe, but these comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: MNIST, one-hidden-layer fully connected network with ReLU and L2 regularization
relationships.reason: R1–R4 show 98.31–98.43% validation accuracy across adaptive methods versus 98.35% for mSGD; the authors describe little accuracy difference.
relationships.display_finding: Reported adaptive validation accuracies near mSGD's 98.35% remain unverified.

relationships.condition: AdamW recovery in the tested CIFAR-10 recipe
relationships.reason: R25 reaches 91.97% versus R23's 93.13% for mSGD, so decoupled weight decay does not recover mSGD accuracy under these settings.
relationships.display_finding: Reported AdamW accuracy below mSGD remains unverified and suggests incomplete recovery under the tested recipe.
